questions.q: In the Black-Scholes Python function, what is `norm.cdf(d1)` used to compute for a call option?
options: The option's gamma
The option's delta
The risk-free discount factor
The option's implied volatility
questions.explain: For a call option, delta equals N(d1), computed in code as norm.cdf(d1) from scipy.stats.

questions.q: Why does the gamma formula use `norm.pdf(d1)` (the normal density) rather than `norm.cdf(d1)` (the cumulative distribution)?
options: Because gamma measures the rate of change of delta, which requires the density function rather than the cumulative probability
Because pdf and cdf always return the same value
Because gamma is only defined for put options
Because norm.cdf cannot be used in Python
questions.explain: Gamma and vega are built from the normal probability density function (pdf), which captures sensitivity/rate-of-change information, while delta itself is built from the cumulative distribution function (cdf).

questions.q: In the worked example, why does Option C (the short put position) contribute a positive amount to portfolio delta, even though its own per-share delta is negative?
options: Because put deltas are always positive in Black-Scholes
Because the position is short, so the negative per-share delta is multiplied by a negative quantity, flipping the sign to positive
Because Option C has the highest strike price in the portfolio
Because gamma offsets delta automatically
questions.explain: Option C's per-share delta is negative (it's a put), but the position quantity itself is negative (short 8 contracts). A negative delta multiplied by a negative position size produces a positive contribution to portfolio delta.

questions.q: How is the hedge trade (`hedge_shares`) calculated from the aggregated Greeks?
options: hedge_shares = portfolio gamma
hedge_shares = portfolio vega divided by 100
hedge_shares = negative of the portfolio delta
hedge_shares = the sum of all strike prices
questions.explain: Since a share of the underlying has a delta of exactly 1, setting hedge_shares equal to the negative of portfolio delta brings the combined position's net delta to zero.

questions.q: Why does the contract multiplier (100 shares per contract) appear in the portfolio Greek calculations?
options: Because each option contract's Greeks must be scaled up to represent the 100 shares of underlying it actually covers
Because Black-Scholes only works for contracts of exactly 100 shares
Because the risk-free rate is always 100 basis points
The multiplier is a typo and should not be included
questions.explain: Black-Scholes delta, gamma, and vega are computed per share of the underlying; since each contract actually represents 100 shares, the per-share Greek must be multiplied by 100 (and by the number of contracts) to get the position-level contribution.
